answer_text:
Since \(A\) is real symmetric, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Thus there is an orthogonal matrix \(Q\) and real numbers \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\) such that

\[
A=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)Q^T.
\]

Hence

\[
A^2=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^2,\dots,\lambda_n^2)Q^T,
\]

so the eigenvalues of \(A^2\) are \(\lambda_i^2\ge 0\).

In the orthonormal eigenbasis of \(A\), the system \(\dot{x}=A^2x\) decouples as

\[
\dot{y}_i=\lambda_i^2 y_i,
\qquad
y_i(t)=e^{\lambda_i^2 t}y_i(0).
\]

If some \(\lambda_k\neq 0\), then \(\lambda_k^2>0\). Choose an initial condition along the corresponding unit eigenvector:

\[
x(0)=\frac{\delta}{2}v_k.
\]

Then \(\|x(0)\|<\delta\), but

\[
\|x(t)\|=\frac{\delta}{2}e^{\lambda_k^2 t}\to \infty.
\]

Thus the zero solution is not stable. Therefore stability forces \(\lambda_i=0\) for all \(i\), which gives \(A=0\).

Conversely, if \(A=0\), then \(\dot{x}=0\), so \(x(t)=x(0)\) and the zero solution is stable.

Thus the only such matrix is

\[
\boxed{A=0_{n\times n}}
\]
